title: “Reading Level” Mostly Means Knowledge Level
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart uses his experience taking the Scholastic Reading Inventory to argue that a student's measured reading level largely reflects vocabulary and background knowledge rather than separable comprehension skills. A sample item shows that without knowing the words, a reader can only guess regardless of how hard they hunt for the main idea, and unfamiliar domain terms such as solar-system vocabulary create the same problem. He concludes that skill drills like find the main idea are far less useful, and far more joyless, than teaching actual content. His remedy is a coherent, knowledge-rich curriculum in history, science, literature, and the arts from the first day of school, which he frames as a matter of equity, pointing readers to Natalie Wexler and Dan Willingham.
points: A reading-level score is mostly a proxy for what words and subject matter a student already knows, not a pure measure of comprehension skill.
Domain vocabulary such as solar-system terms shows how missing background knowledge forces guessing even for strategy-savvy readers.
Strategy lessons help only a little and are boring, so instructional time is better spent on content.
Equity requires a coherent, knowledge-rich curriculum for every child from kindergarten on, including information-rich read-alouds for the youngest.
quotes: You can grit your teeth and try to find the main idea of the passage all day long, but if you don’t know what those words mean (general academic vocabulary words), guess what? You’re going to be guessing.

It’s not that teaching comprehension skills like “find the main idea” is useless — it’s just that they are far less useful than teaching kids actual stuff. And they’re far more boring and joy-killing, too!

The best way to improve reading achievement for all students is to teach history and science and literature and poetry and the arts from a specific, coherent curriculum starting on the very first day of school. The idea that children this young won’t want to hear information-rich read-alouds about Mercury (or Marie Curie, or how farms work, or what the War of 1812 was about) isn’t true.

And what if words like Mercury, Sun, surface, temperature, Fahrenheit, degrees, and atmosphere are unfamiliar to students? These are specific terms used in a particular knowledge domain — the solar system. If you lack background knowledge on the solar system, then again, you’re likely to be guessing.
Equitable educational outcomes (and engagement for all students) cannot happen until we use coherent, knowledge-rich curricula with all children, K-12.
